explorer.trendsDesc: This chart shows how the selected crime type has changed over 16 years across the top 5 countries with the highest average rates. The lines help identify long-term trends — whether crime is increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable in different regions.

explorer.yearToYearDesc: This heatmap shows how crime rates changed from one year to the next across Europe. Green means crime decreased, red means crime increased. Values show percentage change compared to the previous year.
explorer.fingerprints: Criminal Fingerprints: Country vs European Average
explorer.fingerprintsDesc: This heatmap compares each country's crime rates to the European average (2019-2023 data). Green means below average, red means above average. Values show how many times higher or lower than the EU average (1.0 = exactly average). This visualization reveals each country's unique "criminal fingerprint" — their distinctive pattern of crime types.
explorer.posterDesc: View the full project analysis poster summarizing key findings and visualizations (PDF)

overview.title: Overview
overview.content: This project explores crime trends across European countries using publicly available data from Eurostat and provides a reproducible exploratory analysis of crime patterns across Europe. The objective was to apply core data science skills — data cleaning, preprocessing, exploratory analysis, visualization, and interpretation — to produce meaningful insights about crime patterns.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.content: The project uses crime categories defined by the ICCS (International Classification of Crime Statistics) framework, allowing consistent comparison across countries and years. Crime rates are normalized per 100,000 inhabitants to enable fair comparison between countries of different population sizes. This project is purely descriptive and does not make causal claims.

scope.title: Scope & Limitations
scope.content: This project covers 25 crime categories across 39 European countries, mainly from 2008 to 2023, but also using historic data from 1993-2007. Note that reporting practices and legal definitions vary between countries, which may affect comparability. Some data points may be missing or show anomalies due to differences in national reporting systems.

insights.title: Key Findings
insights.subtitle: Notable patterns and observations discovered during the analysis of European crime data.
insights.disclaimer: These are analytical observations based on the data. They reflect patterns we identified, but may not capture the full picture. Differences in national reporting practices, legal definitions, and data availability can influence the results.

property-crime-decline.title: Property Crime is Declining Across Europe
property-crime-decline.description: Burglary, robbery, and theft show consistent 10-15 year downward trends across most European countries. This may be connected to improved security technology (surveillance cameras, alarm systems), the shift towards a cashless society, and people carrying less valuable items in public.

modern-crime-rise.title: Modern Crime Types are on the Rise
modern-crime-rise.description: Acts against computer systems, money laundering, and drug-related offences show upward trends since 2016. This likely reflects both the actual growth of digital and organized crime, and improved detection capabilities by law enforcement — better banking surveillance, automated scanning tools, and dedicated cybercrime units.

sexual-violence-reporting.title: Sexual Violence Statistics Reflect Reporting Culture
sexual-violence-reporting.description: Countries like Sweden show among the highest sexual violence rates in Europe, particularly after 2018. This is largely attributed to consent-based legislation (Sweden's 2018 law), the #MeToo movement increasing willingness to report, and broader legal definitions of sexual offences. Higher recorded rates in these countries likely reflect better detection and reporting, not necessarily higher actual crime.

baltic-homicide-decline.title: Sharp Homicide Decline in the Baltic States
baltic-homicide-decline.description: Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia were among Europe's highest-rate countries for intentional homicide in 2008, but have seen dramatic declines since then. This suggests societal stabilization, economic development, and the narrowing of the gap between Baltic and Western European safety levels.

post-covid-surge.title: Post-COVID Surge in Theft and Robbery
post-covid-surge.description: After a drop during COVID-19 lockdowns (2020-2021), theft and robbery rates began climbing again from 2022 onwards. This coincides with the return of public activity, tourism, and crowded spaces — conditions that create more opportunities for these types of crime.

small-country-effect.title: Small Countries Show Volatile Statistics
small-country-effect.description: Countries with very small populations (like Liechtenstein) can show extreme per-capita rates due to small absolute numbers. A handful of incidents can dramatically shift the per 100,000 rate, making these countries appear as outliers when they may not represent a genuine safety concern.

fraud-replacing-theft.title: Fraud is Replacing Theft as the Top Crime
fraud-replacing-theft.description: In Spain and Poland, fraud has overtaken theft as the most common crime type in recent years (around 2017-2021). This structural shift reflects the move towards online commerce and digital transactions, creating new opportunities for fraud while reducing traditional theft.

finland-cybercrime.title: Cybercrime Spike in Recent Years
finland-cybercrime.description: Finland shows a notable spike in acts against computer systems in 2022-2023. This could be related to legislative changes, new detection software, or increased reporting of cyber incidents.

drugs-top-crime.title: Drug Offences Have Risen to the Top
drugs-top-crime.description: In some countries, unlawful acts involving controlled drugs have become the most frequently recorded crime type. This may reflect changes in police enforcement priorities and border control practices rather than necessarily higher drug consumption.
